perception-s1.title: Three perception figures: grouping, a road scene and an illusion

perception-s2.title: What you expect shapes what you see
perception-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether recent experience changes how people perceive an ambiguous drawing: a sketch that can be seen either as a rat or as a man with glasses.

Participants

80 college students (ages 18-22) at one university volunteered. Each gave informed consent and was told they could stop at any time.

Method

Students were randomly assigned to one of two groups of 40. The animal group first looked at six drawings of animals; the face group first looked at six drawings of faces. Then every student saw the same ambiguous drawing for five seconds and wrote down what it showed. At the end, each student was told the purpose of the study.

Results

In the animal group, 31 of 40 students reported seeing a rat. In the face group, 9 of 40 reported seeing a rat; the rest reported a man.

Discussion

The researchers concluded that the drawings seen first changed what students perceived in the same picture.

Invented study for practice.

thinking-s1.title: Same facts, different wording
thinking-s1.html: Sixty adults read about a surgery and decided whether they would choose it. A computer randomly assigned each person to one of two versions. Half (30) read that 90% of patients survive the surgery; the other half (30) read that 10% of patients die from it. The graph shows the percent in each version who chose the surgery.

thinking-s2.title: The candle problem and the box of tacks
thinking-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether seeing an object in its usual role makes it harder to use it in a new way. Participants had to attach a candle to a wall so it could burn without dripping wax on the table, using a candle, a book of matches and a box of thumbtacks. The solution is to empty the box, tack it to the wall and use it as a shelf.

Participants

48 high school juniors from two schools took part with written parental permission and their own agreement. Each was told they could stop at any time.

Method

Students were randomly assigned to one of two groups of 24. In the full-box group, the tacks were given inside the box. In the empty-box group, the tacks were given beside the empty box. Each student worked alone, and a researcher timed how many minutes the student took to reach the solution, up to 10 minutes.

Results

The empty-box group solved the problem in an average of 2 minutes; the full-box group took an average of 6 minutes, and 7 of its students did not solve it within 10 minutes.

Discussion

The researchers concluded that seeing the box as a container made it harder to see it as a shelf.

Invented study for practice.

memory-intro-s1.title: Thinking about meaning and remembering words
memory-intro-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers tested whether the kind of question people answer about a word changes how well they remember it later.

Participants

90 adults (ages 18-60) recruited through a community library took part. All gave informed consent, and the consent form explained they could withdraw at any time.

Method

Each participant saw the same 40 words, one at a time, and answered one yes-or-no question about each. A computer randomly assigned each participant to one of three conditions (30 per condition). Letters condition: "Is the word in capital letters?" Rhyme condition: "Does the word rhyme with train?" Meaning condition: "Would the word fit in the sentence She put the ___ on the table?" Participants were not told there would be a memory test. Twenty minutes later they were given a surprise test: a list of 80 words (the 40 they saw and 40 new ones), and they marked each word they had seen.

Results

The letters group correctly marked 15% of the words they had seen, the rhyme group 45%, and the meaning group 78%.

Discussion

Afterward, every participant was told why the test had been a surprise and could ask to have their data removed.

Invented study for practice.

memory-intro-s2.title: Two tasks at once
memory-intro-s2.html:
Percent of digits recalled in order, by what students did while holding the digits (invented data for practice)
During the 20 secondsDigits recalled
Nothing86%
Repeating "the the the"52%
Tapping a visual pattern80%

Forty students held a list of 7 spoken digits in mind for 20 seconds, then said them back. During the 20 seconds, every student did each of three things on different trials: nothing, repeating "the the the" out loud, or tapping a pattern on a keypad they could see. The table shows the percent of digits recalled in order.

encoding-memories-s1.title: A serial position curve from a recall study
encoding-memories-s1.html: Sixty students heard a list of 15 unrelated words, one every two seconds, and then wrote down as many as they could in any order. A computer randomly assigned half the students to write the words right away. The other half first counted backward by threes for 30 seconds, which kept them from repeating the words to themselves. The graph shows the percent of students in each group who recalled the word at each position.

encoding-memories-s2.title: Spaced or massed study of new vocabulary
encoding-memories-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether spreading study sessions out over time helps students remember vocabulary longer than doing the same amount of study all at once.

Participants

64 tenth graders in Spanish 1 classes at a public high school in Texas. Parents gave written permission and students agreed to take part; the school's review committee approved the study.

Method

Students were randomly assigned to two groups of 32. Both groups studied the same 30 new Spanish words for three 15-minute sessions. The massed group did all three sessions on one Monday, back to back. The spaced group did one session each Monday for three weeks. Four weeks after each group's last session, all students took the same test: they saw each English word and wrote the Spanish word.

Results

On the final test, the spaced group wrote an average of 18 of 30 words correctly (60%); the massed group wrote an average of 10 of 30 (about 33%).

Discussion

The researchers concluded that spacing study sessions improves long-term retention of vocabulary.

Invented study for practice.

storing-memories-s1.title: A patient who cannot keep new memories
storing-memories-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers described one patient in depth to learn which kinds of memory survive damage to the hippocampus.

Participants

One patient, called R.T. in the report to protect his identity: a 58-year-old retired electrician whose hippocampus on both sides was damaged by a brain infection. R.T. and his wife both gave written informed consent.

Method

Over 18 months the researchers interviewed R.T. and his wife, reviewed his medical records and brain scans, and gave him memory tests. On each of five days he also practiced tracing a star while seeing his hand only in a mirror, and the researchers timed each attempt.

Results

R.T. could not recall the researchers from one visit to the next or name anything that had happened since the infection. He recalled his childhood, his wedding and his years at work in detail. Memories of the two years just before the infection were patchy. His mirror-tracing time fell from 90 seconds on day 1 to 35 seconds on day 5, though each day he said he had never done the task.

Discussion

The researchers concluded that the hippocampus is needed to form new explicit memories but not to keep old ones or to learn new skills.

Invented study for practice.

storing-memories-s2.title: Repeating words versus linking them to meaning
storing-memories-s2.html: Fifty college students studied the same 20 words for the same length of time. A coin flip assigned each student to one of two instructions: repeat each word over and over, or think of a personal memory linked to each word. The next day, without warning, every student wrote down all the words they could remember.

retrieving-memories-s1.title: Same room, better memory?
retrieving-memories-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether people remember more when they are tested in the same place where they learned.

Participants

48 college students (ages 18-23) at a university in Ohio volunteered for course credit. Each signed an informed consent form and was told they could leave at any time without losing credit; a university review board approved the study.

Method

Every student learned a list of 30 words in Room A, a small room with blue walls and a smell of peppermint. A day later, a computer randomly assigned half the students to be tested in Room A again and half in Room B, a large gray room with no smell. In both rooms the students had five minutes to write down as many of the words as they could.

Results

Students tested in Room A wrote down 17 of the 30 words on average; students tested in Room B wrote down 12.

Discussion

The researchers concluded that being in the learning environment helped students retrieve the words.

Invented study for practice.

retrieving-memories-s2.title: Quizzing or rereading before a unit test
retrieving-memories-s2.html:
Percent correct on the same unit test, one week after a lesson, by review method (invented data for practice)
Review methodNumber of studentsPercent correct on the unit testStudents' own prediction of their score
Reread the notes twice4561%78%

A teacher randomly assigned 90 ninth graders to review a science lesson in one of two ways for the same 20 minutes. Just before the unit test, each student predicted what percent they would score.

forgetting-s1.title: Eyewitness memory and a leading question
forgetting-s1.html:
Introduction

Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer asked whether the wording of a question about an event can change what a witness later remembers about it.

Participants

150 university students in the United States took part in groups.

Method

Every student watched the same short film of a multiple-car accident, then answered questions about it. One group of 50 was asked, "About how fast were the cars going when they smashed into each other?" A second group of 50 was asked the same question with hit instead of smashed into. A control group of 50 was not asked about speed. One week later, all students returned and answered more questions without seeing the film again, including "Did you see any broken glass?" There was no broken glass in the film.

Results

Yes, they had seen broken glass: 16 of 50 students in the smashed group, 7 of 50 in the hit group and 6 of 50 in the control group.

Discussion

The authors argued that the verb "smashed" changed students' memory of the accident itself, adding a detail that was not there.

Loftus, E. F., & Palmer, J. C. (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 13, 585-589.

forgetting-s2.title: What a second list does to the first
forgetting-s2.html: Forty students learned List A, 20 pairs of words. A coin flip assigned half to rest for 20 minutes and half to spend those 20 minutes learning List B, 20 different pairs using the same first words. Then every student was tested on List A only.

intelligence-s2.title: A reminder before a math test
intelligence-s2.html:
Introduction

Researchers tested whether reminding students of a negative stereotype about their group before a hard math test lowers their scores.

Participants

120 women in their first year at two public universities, all of whom had taken calculus in high school. Each gave informed consent; the universities' review boards approved the study.

Method

A computer randomly assigned each woman to one of two groups of 60. Before the test, the reminder group read: "This test has shown gender differences in past research." The no-reminder group read: "This test has shown no gender differences in past research." Everyone then took the same 20-question math test in 20 minutes. Afterward, every participant was told the true purpose of the two statements and that neither was a real research finding.

Results

The reminder group answered 9.1 questions correctly on average (SD 3.0); the no-reminder group answered 11.4 (SD 3.2). The difference was statistically significant.

Discussion

The researchers concluded that a stereotype reminder lowered math performance in this sample.

Invented study for practice.

items.q: In Figure A every shape is the same distance from its neighbors, yet most people see six columns rather than six rows. Which Gestalt principle explains this?
options: Similarity: shapes that look alike are grouped together
Proximity: shapes that are close together are grouped
Closure: gaps in an outline are filled in to make a whole
Figure-ground: one part stands out against a background

items.q: In Figure B the two blue people have the same shape, but one is drawn much smaller. Which depth cue makes the smaller one look farther away rather than tiny?
In Figure B the box covers part of the orange person. Which depth cue tells a viewer that the box is closer than the person?
In Figure C the two orange bars are the same length, but the upper bar looks longer. Which explanation fits the most common account of this illusion?
options: The upper bar sits closer to the eyes, so retinal disparity between the two eyes makes it look larger
Change blindness hides the true length of the lower bar, so the viewer underestimates it and sees it as shorter
The lower bar is seen through the cocktail party effect and so attracts less notice
The converging lines act as a depth cue, so the upper bar is judged farther away and size constancy makes it look larger

items.q: Which research method did this study use?
How did this study operationally define what a student perceived?
options: The set of six animal or face drawings each group saw first
What the student wrote down after five seconds with the drawing
How strong the student's expectations felt inside
Which group the student was randomly assigned to

items.q: What percent of the animal group reported seeing a rat?

mistakes.why: 38.75% divides by all 80 students. The question asks about the animal group only, so divide by its 40.
22.5% is the face group (9 of 40). Use the animal group's 31.

items.q: Which concept best explains the difference between the two groups?
At a loud party, Keisha is talking with a friend and hears nothing of the other conversations, until someone across the room says her name. Which concept does this show?
A film editor swaps an actor's red scarf for a blue one between two shots. Most viewers do not notice. Which concept explains this?
A proofreader reads "the the cat" as "the cat" because she knows what the sentence should say. Which kind of processing is she relying on?
A baby who has never seen a giraffe looks at its lines, colors and edges and slowly builds an image of the animal. Which process is this?
As a friend walks away from you down a hallway, the image of her on your retina shrinks, but she does not seem to be getting smaller. Which concept explains this?
When Dev holds a pencil a few inches from his nose, he feels his eyes turn inward. Which depth cue is this?
A movie is a rapid series of still frames, yet viewers see smooth motion. Which concept explains this?
In a well-known study, people counting basketball passes in a video often missed a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. What does this show about attention?
options: People perceive everything in a scene, including the gorilla, but forget it within seconds
Focusing attention on one task can make people miss an object in plain view
Motion in a scene is hard for the eyes to detect
Wearing a costume makes a person blend into a background

items.q: Both versions give the same survival odds. Which concept explains why the choices differed?
In the "10% die" version, 12 of the 30 people chose the surgery. Check the graph: what percent is that?

mistakes.why: 20% divides by all 60 people. Only 30 read the "10% die" version, so divide by 30.
12 is the count of people, not a percent. Divide by 30 and multiply by 100.

items.q: Why can the researchers conclude that the wording caused the difference in choices?
options: Sixty adults is enough people to prove any result is true
Chance alone decided which version each person read, so the groups were alike except for the wording
The people chose freely, so their answers show their real preferences
Both versions were read on a computer screen in the same lab room

items.q: Which concept best explains why the full-box group took longer?
What was the operational definition of problem-solving performance in this study?
options: Whether the tacks came inside or beside the box
How creative each student felt during the task
The number of students who were in each of the groups
Minutes a student took to reach the solution, up to 10

items.q: Which ethical safeguard does the summary describe, and how was it applied?
options: Informed assent and permission: parents gave written permission and each student agreed to take part
Debriefing after deception: students were told the true purpose after a cover story
Random assignment: each student had an equal chance of being in either group
Confidentiality: names were replaced with code numbers before analysis

items.q: A student in the full-box group first tried to melt wax to glue the candle to the wall, then kept trying versions of that same idea. Which concept describes this second problem?
Asked to picture a "bird", most people imagine something like a robin, not a penguin. A robin is the bird category's what?
A child calls every four-legged animal at the farm a "dog". Later she learns that cows and horses are different, and she makes new categories for them. What is the second step?
Ana needs to find a misspelled name in a list of 500, so she checks every name, one by one, against the class roster. Which strategy is she using?
After a week of news stories about a plane crash, Jordan decides to drive across the country instead of flying, though driving is far more dangerous per mile. Which concept explains his judgment?
Told that a quiet man loves poetry, most people guess he is a classics professor rather than a truck driver, even though there are far more truck drivers. Which concept explains the guess?
A roulette wheel has landed on red seven times in a row. Malik bets on black, sure it is "due". Which concept describes his error?
Priya has paid for a concert ticket. On the night she is sick and would rather stay home, but she goes anyway because "I already paid for it." Which concept explains her choice?
Students who first read a list including the word "ocean" are faster to recognize the word "wave" a minute later. Which concept explains this?
In a brainstorming session, Leo is asked to list as many uses for a brick as he can in two minutes. Which kind of thinking is the task measuring?

After damage to her prefrontal cortex, a patient can still define words and do arithmetic but struggles to plan a meal, switch between tasks and stop herself from interrupting. Which abilities are most affected?
Which concept do the results best support?
options: Levels of processing: thinking about meaning leads to better memory
Procedural memory: practicing a skill makes it automatic
Prospective memory: people remember planned actions better than words
Sensory memory: words held for a moment are fully stored

items.q: How did this study operationally define memory for the words?
options: The type of question a participant answered about each word
The percent of seen words correctly marked on the 80-word list
How deeply a participant thought about the words while reading
The amount of time between seeing the words and the test

items.q: Each participant saw 40 words. On average, how many of those 40 words did the meaning group mark correctly?

mistakes.why: 62.4 uses all 80 words on the test list. Only 40 of them had been seen, and the percent is of those 40.
78 is the percent, not a number of words. Take 78% of the 40 words seen.

items.q: The participants were not told about the memory test in advance. Which safeguard in the summary addresses this?
options: Random assignment: a computer placed each participant in one of the three conditions
Confidentiality: participants' names were removed from the data files
Debriefing: afterward each person learned why the test was a surprise
Animal care review: an animal welfare committee approved the procedure

items.q: Repeating "the the the" hurt digit recall much more than tapping a pattern. Which part of working memory best explains this?
options: The visuospatial sketchpad, which holds images and places
Long-term memory, which has a very large capacity
Sensory memory, which holds sounds for a few seconds
The phonological loop, which holds words and sounds

items.q: By how many percentage points was recall lower when repeating "the the the" than when doing nothing?

mistakes.why: 6 compares doing nothing with tapping. The question compares doing nothing with repeating words.
28 compares tapping with repeating. Compare repeating with doing nothing (86%).

items.q: Every student did all three tasks, on different trials. What is the main advantage of this design?
options: Each student is compared with themselves, so personal ability is held constant
It lets the researchers generalize the results to adults in many different cultures and settings
It turns the study into a correlational study of tasks and recall
It removes the need for an operational definition of recall

items.q: Maya remembers her eighth birthday party, the cake and who was there. Which kind of memory is this?
Ravi knows that Paris is the capital of France but cannot remember when or where he learned it. Which kind of memory holds this fact?
Years after learning, Lena types quickly without thinking about where the keys are, but she cannot say where the letter G is without picturing a keyboard. Which kind of memory lets her type?
On his way home, Omar remembers that he promised to pick up bread. Which kind of memory is he using?
A student walks out of a party and, without trying, knows roughly how long she stayed and which room was busiest. Which kind of processing explains this?
In rats, repeatedly stimulating a pathway in the hippocampus makes its synapses respond more strongly for weeks afterward, and blocking this change impairs learning. Which concept is this?
Put the stages of the multi-store model in the order information passes through them.
A patient with damage to the hippocampus cannot form new memories of events, yet over several days gets faster at tracing a star in a mirror without remembering ever practicing. What does this show?
options: Memory is stored in one single brain system, so the patient's impairment is mild
Procedural memory needs conscious awareness of each earlier practice session
Short-term memory is unaffected, so the practice is being held in sensory memory
Explicit and implicit memory depend partly on different brain systems

items.q: In the "recall right away" group, words 1 to 3 were recalled more often than words 6 to 10. Which concept names this part of the curve?
For word 15, how many percentage points lower was recall after 30 seconds of counting than right away?

mistakes.why: 2 is the difference for word 1, at the other end of the list. Read the points for word 15.
88% is only the "right away" value for word 15. Subtract the "after counting" value, 32%.

items.q: The 30-second counting task almost erased the recency effect but barely changed the primacy effect. Which explanation fits best?
options: Counting improved encoding of the first words, which raised the primacy effect
Counting pushed the last words out of short-term memory; early words were already in long-term memory
The early words were held in sensory memory, which lasts longer than short-term memory
The students in the counting group were less motivated, so they recalled fewer words overall

items.q: Why could the researchers say the counting task caused the drop in recall of the last words?
options: The study measured recall for 15 different word positions instead of one
Sixty students took part, which is enough to prove the effect is real
Random assignment made the groups alike except for the counting task
The words were unrelated, so no student could group them into meaningful units

items.q: Which concept do the results support?
Which is the independent variable in this study?
options: Whether the three study sessions were on one day or over three weeks
The number of Spanish words written correctly on the final test
The 30 Spanish words that both groups of tenth graders studied
The four weeks between the last session and the final test

items.q: A school board member wants to use these results for adults learning Spanish at night school. Which point about the participants matters most for that generalization?
options: The study had 64 students, which is too small a sample to generalize from
The participants were tenth graders in one Texas school, unlike adults
The students were randomly assigned, so the results apply to learners of any age
The final test was given four weeks after the last session

items.q: Which ethical safeguard does the summary describe for these minors?
options: Debriefing after a cover story about the true purpose
Payment to each student for each of the study sessions
Parental permission plus each student's own agreement
Random assignment of students to the two study schedules

items.q: To remember a 10-digit phone number, Kenji remembers it as an area code, a three-digit prefix and four digits. Which strategy is he using?
To memorize a speech, Aisha pictures walking through her house and places each point in a different room. During the speech she "walks" through the rooms. Which mnemonic is this?
Studying for a biology test, Sam organizes his notes as an outline: "Cells" at the top, then "Plant cells" and "Animal cells", then the parts of each. Which encoding strategy is he using?
Students learn the colors of the rainbow as "ROY G BIV". What kind of memory aid is this?
Jada studies for six hours straight the night before her exam and does fine the next day, but a month later she remembers little. Which concept describes how she studied?

A hiring manager interviews eight candidates in one day. At the end of the day, she remembers the last two clearly but the middle ones blur together. Which concept explains her clear memory of the last two?
Two students each have three hours to study for a final exam four weeks away. Which plan is most likely to lead to the best memory on exam day?
options: One three-hour session the night before the exam
Six 30-minute sessions spread across the four weeks
One three-hour session four weeks before the exam
Three one-hour sessions on the same Saturday morning

items.q: On a test of his memory, Arjun can hold about seven single letters, but he can hold far more letters when they form the words of a sentence. Which concept explains the difference?
options: The method of loci gives each letter its own imagined place
The primacy effect makes the first letters in a sentence easier
Chunking turns many letters into a few meaningful units
Massed practice of the sentence made it easier to repeat

items.q: Which research method did the researchers use?
R.T. cannot form memories of anything that happened after the infection. Which concept names this?
R.T.'s mirror-tracing time fell over five days though he did not remember practicing. Which conclusion does this best support?
options: His anterograde amnesia went away by day 5
Mirror tracing is stored in sensory memory
Procedural memory can form without the hippocampus
Old explicit memories are needed to learn a skill

items.q: How did the researchers apply the ethical guideline of confidentiality?
options: They gave R.T. five separate days to practice the mirror-tracing task
They reviewed R.T.'s medical records and his brain scans
They randomly assigned R.T. to the mirror-tracing condition
They called him R.T. in the report so he could not be identified

items.q: Which concept describes what the second group did with each word?
Each student studied 20 words. On average, how many of the 20 words did the "link each word to a memory" group recall?

mistakes.why: 4.4 uses the "repeat each word" bar (22%). Read the "link each word to a memory" bar, 58%.
58 is the percent, not the number of words. Take 58% of the 20 words.

items.q: Which statement best explains why linking words to memories led to better recall a day later?
options: Repeating words keeps them in short-term memory, which can last for several days
Linking words to meaning ties them to stored memories, encoding them more deeply
Linking words to memories gave that group more total time to study
The second group knew a memory test was coming the next day

items.q: Waiting to pay, Elena repeats a new friend's phone number over and over until she types it into her phone. A week later she cannot recall it. Which kind of rehearsal did she use?
After a car crash, Marcus cannot remember the week before the accident, though he forms new memories normally. Which concept describes his memory loss?
Most adults can recall almost nothing from before about age 3, though they experienced many events then. Which concept names this?
A woman can tell you what she did on almost any date in the last 30 years, including the day of the week and what was in the news, without using a diary or memory tricks. Which concept describes her?
options: The method of loci, a mnemonic

items.q: A 74-year-old man has more and more trouble remembering conversations from the same morning, then over several years also struggles with names of family members and with daily tasks. Brain scans show the hippocampus shrinking first. Which condition best fits?
options: Retrograde amnesia from a single head injury

items.q: Students who sleep after learning a list of word pairs remember more of them the next day than students who stay awake for the same hours. Which process does sleep most likely help?
A boxer is knocked out. Afterward he remembers the fight's first round but not the knockout punch or the minutes before it. Which explanation best fits?
options: The last minutes had not yet been consolidated into long-term memory
He has infantile amnesia for the knockout
The knockout punch was stored by maintenance rehearsal
The first round was in sensory memory, so it lasted longer

items.q: Studying for a quiz, Noor explains each new term to herself in her own words and gives an example from her own life. Which kind of rehearsal is she using?
Which concept do the results best support?
What was the operational definition of memory in this study?
options: Whether the student was tested in Room A or in Room B
The number of the 30 words written down in five minutes
How familiar the testing room felt to each student
The blue walls and peppermint smell of Room A

items.q: What percent of the 30 words did the students tested in Room A write down on average?

mistakes.why: 40% is Room B (12 of 30). The question asks about Room A, 17 of 30.
17 is the number of words, not a percent. Divide by 30 and multiply by 100.

items.q: Which safeguard described in the summary protected the students' freedom to stop?
options: Students were randomly assigned to be tested in Room A or Room B
Students were told the true purpose after a cover story
Students could leave at any time without losing course credit
Students' names were kept in a locked file

items.q: Which concept do the test scores show?
By how many percentage points did the rereading group overpredict its own score?

mistakes.why: 13 is how much the quiz group underpredicted. The question asks about the rereading group.
18 compares the two groups' actual scores. Compare the rereading group's prediction with its own score.

items.q: The rereading group predicted a higher score than the quiz group but actually scored lower. Which concept best explains the mistaken predictions?
options: Poor metacognition: rereading feels familiar, which students mistake for knowing
State-dependent memory: the students were in a different body state when predicting
Mood-congruent memory: the rereaders felt more cheerful, so they predicted high
Recognition: students recognized the notes, so their predictions were accurate

items.q: On a test, Grace cannot answer "Name the four lobes of the cerebral cortex," but on a later question she easily picks the occipital lobe from a list of options. Which concept explains the difference?
Walking into the kitchen, Tom forgets why he came. He goes back to the couch where he had the thought, and it comes back to him. Which concept explains this?
In a study, people who learned a list while they had drunk caffeine recalled it best when they had caffeine again at the test. Which concept does this show?
After a breakup, Jaylen finds that sad memories from years ago keep coming to mind, while happy ones feel far away. Which concept explains this?
Rather than rereading her notes, Fatima covers them and writes down everything she can remember about each heading, then checks what she missed. Which strategy is she using?
A friend shows Ben a photo of the beach where they vacationed, and a flood of details about the trip come back. In this example the photo acts as what?
Before an exam, Leo looks over his notes, thinks "I know all of this", and stops studying. On the exam he cannot recall much of it. Which skill would most help Leo avoid this?
options: Mood-congruent memory: studying in a happy mood
Infantile amnesia: forgetting the earliest material first
Recognition: rereading the notes until each line looks familiar
Metacognition: checking what he knows by testing himself

items.q: A teacher replaces end-of-class review with a short, ungraded quiz on the day's lesson. A month later, her students remember more than last year's class, who reviewed by rereading. Which concept best explains the improvement?
What was the independent variable in this study?
options: The verb used in the question about speed
Whether the student reported seeing broken glass
The film of the accident that the students watched
The one week between the film and the second session

items.q: What percent of the smashed group reported seeing broken glass?

mistakes.why: About 10.7% divides by all 150 students. Only 50 were in the smashed group.
14% is the hit group (7 of 50). The question asks about the smashed group.

items.q: Which concept do the results best support?
Which point about the participants most limits applying this result to real eyewitnesses of a crash?
options: The study had 150 students, too few to generalize from
The three groups heard different questions after the film
They were students watching a film, not witnesses to a real crash
The students answered the questions a week after the film

items.q: Which concept explains the lower recall of List A in the group that learned List B?
By how many percentage points was List A recall lower after learning List B than after resting?

mistakes.why: 45% is the List B group's recall, not the difference. Subtract it from the rest group's 70%.
115 adds the bars. The question asks how much lower one is, so subtract.

items.q: Why did the comparison group rest for the same 20 minutes instead of being tested on List A right away?
options: So both groups had the same delay and differed just in learning List B
So the rest group could rehearse List A for longer
So the study would be correlational instead of an experiment
So the students would not know which list would be tested

items.q: Ines memorized her new locker combination this year, but when she tries to open her locker she keeps entering last year's combination. Which concept explains this?
After a year of studying French, Kai finds that the Spanish words he learned in ninth grade are harder to recall; French words keep coming to mind instead. Which concept explains this?
Most people cannot draw the front of a penny accurately, though they have seen thousands. Which concept best explains this?
Asked for the name of an actor, Dana says "It starts with a B, two syllables, I can almost see it," but she cannot produce the name. An hour later it comes to her. Which concept describes this?
Rosa tells a funny story at dinner, sure it happened to her cousin. Later she realizes she read it online. Which concept describes her error?
Asked to vividly imagine getting lost in a mall as a child several times, some adults later become more confident that it really happened. Which concept describes this?
Two friends remember the same argument very differently, each sure their version is accurate. Which idea best explains how both can be confident?
options: Proactive interference: an earlier argument between the same two friends blocks this one
Encoding failure: neither friend stored any part of it
Infantile amnesia: early memories are hard to retrieve
Constructive memory: each rebuilt the event, filling gaps with expectations

items.q: A therapist sees a client who cannot remember a frightening event from childhood. From the psychodynamic perspective, what is the explanation?
options: Repression: the threatening memory was pushed out of awareness
Proactive interference: earlier learning blocked the later event
Encoding failure: the child did not pay attention to the event
The misinformation effect: someone gave the client false details

items.q: Ebbinghaus found that he forgot much of a list of nonsense syllables within the first hour, then forgot more slowly over the next month. Which concept describes this pattern?
Malia scores 130 on this test. What is her z score?

mistakes.why: 30 is how many points above the mean she is. Divide by the standard deviation, 15, to get z.

About 8.7 divides the raw score by 15. Subtract the mean first: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>130</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">130 - 100 = 30</annotation></semantics></math>, then divide by 15.

items.q: By the 68-95-99.7 rule, what percent of people score between 85 and 115?

mistakes.why: 34% is only one side, from 100 to 115. Add the other side, 85 to 100.
95% is within two standard deviations (70 to 130). 85 to 115 is within one.

items.q: By the 68-95-99.7 rule, what percent of people score above 130 (the shaded region)?

mistakes.why: 5% is outside two standard deviations on both sides. Only the upper side is shaded, so halve it.
13.5% is the band from 115 to 130. The shaded region starts at 130.

items.q: Jonah's score is at the 84th percentile. What does that mean?
options: He scored higher than about 84% of the norm group
He answered about 84% of the test items correctly
His IQ score is 84 points on this test
He scored lower than about 84% of the norm group

items.q: What IQ score is one standard deviation below the mean on this test?

mistakes.why: 115 is one standard deviation above the mean. Below the mean, subtract 15.

84 is the percentile one standard deviation above the mean. The question asks for a score: <math class="psy-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100 - 15</annotation></semantics></math>.

items.q: Which concept do the results best support?
What does "the difference was statistically significant" mean here?
options: The difference is large enough to matter in everyday life
Each woman in the reminder group scored lower than each woman in the other group
A difference this large would be unlikely if chance alone were at work
The result will be found again by any lab that repeats the study

items.q: The participants were given a false statement about past research. Which safeguard in the summary addressed this?
options: Random assignment: a computer placed each woman in a group
Confidentiality: the test scores were stored without any names
Protection from harm: the math test lasted twenty minutes
Debriefing: afterward each woman learned the statements were false

items.q: A reader wants to apply this result to all high school girls taking math tests. Which statement about generalizing is best supported?
options: Partly: they were female math students, but older and in college
Fully, because 120 women is a large enough sample
No, because the study was a true experiment
Fully, because the women were randomly assigned to groups

items.q: Students who do well on vocabulary tests also tend to do well on math, puzzle and memory tests. Which idea does this pattern support?
options: Multiple intelligences that are fully separate

items.q: On an early intelligence test, a child aged 8 performs like a typical 10-year-old. Using the original IQ formula (mental age divided by chronological age, times 100), what is the child's IQ?

mistakes.why: 80 divides chronological age by mental age. Put mental age (10) on top.
1.25 is the ratio. Multiply by 100 to get the IQ.

items.q: A group of students takes the same intelligence test twice, a month apart, and their two scores correlate at r = .92. What does this show about the test?
A college admissions test is given to applicants, and their scores correlate r = .45 with their first-year college grades. What property of the test does this correlation measure?
Before a new test is used, it is given in the same way to a large, representative sample, whose scores become the norms for comparing later test takers. What is this process called?
In many countries, average raw scores on intelligence tests rose by about 3 IQ points per decade during the 20th century, so tests had to be renormed. Which concept names this?
Which test is an achievement test rather than an aptitude test?
options: A test designed to predict who will do well in law school
A test of how quickly someone could learn a new language
A final exam on what was taught in a semester of chemistry
A test used to predict success in pilot training

items.q: After a low score on a math quiz, Tae says, "I am just not a math person," and stops studying. His friend says, "I need a different strategy and more practice." Which concept describes the friend's view?

Seeds from one bag are planted in two fields, one with rich soil and one with poor soil. Within each field, height differences are mostly due to the seeds' genes. Which conclusion about the difference between the two fields is correct?
options: It can be caused by the soil, though variation within a field is genetic
It is genetic, because the differences within each field are genetic
It is not measurable, because the two fields used different kinds of soil
It is mostly random, because the seeds came from one single bag

items.q: In 1917 the US Army gave intelligence tests to recruits, including many recent immigrants who spoke little English. Lower scores were later used to argue for limits on immigration from certain countries. What was the central problem?
options: The tests were too reliable to be useful for any purpose
The tests measured English and American culture, not just ability
The recruits had been randomly assigned to take the tests
The Flynn effect made the scores rise too fast for comparison
